video_title: The Fed Is Hiking Into A Growth Slowdown | Weekly Roundup
gist: Forward Guidance's weekly roundup with hosts Felix and Quinn plus guest Vincent Deluard of StoneX, recorded just after a unanimous 25bp Fed hike under new chair Kevin Warsh. The first half argues the Fed is turning most hawkish precisely at peak growth, as roughly $300-400bn of 'stealth midterm stimulus' (SPR draining, tariff refunds, tax refunds, accelerated capex deductions) rolls off into a likely Democratic midterm sweep, leaving a stagflationary economy with six months of negative real wages and a dead housing market. The second half departs from the title entirely: Deluard lays out a decade-long macro call that Europe is Japan circa 2012 and must debase the euro, with trade expressions in long yen/long USD/long BRL versus short euro, a contrarian long in hated UK equities, and a bullish read on Carney's Canada.

insights.claim: The Fed under new chair Kevin Warsh delivered a unanimous 25bp hike, and the lack of dispersion in the dot plot surprised the Forward Guidance hosts, who expected more committee disagreement between stopping at two hikes and going to a third.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: A unanimous hawkish committee removes the 'dissent' tell traders normally use to fade a cycle; positioning for an early pause has less institutional support than assumed.
insights.quote: the most surprising thing for me was how unanimous it was. Everybody voted for the hike which was quite surprising to me

insights.claim: Vincent Deluard publicly admitted he was wrong on two calls going into the meeting: he expected a dovish hike and expected Warsh to fumble the press conference, and instead judged Warsh's command of the room as materially improved.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: The 'Warsh is an unserious communicator' short thesis has been invalidated; expect his pressers to move markets more, not less.
insights.quote: I expected a doubbish hike and uh I expected uh Kevin Walsh to fumble the press conference and the truth is I was wrong on both counts

insights.claim: October is underpriced at roughly 50% odds of a hike, because the Fed has said it has only removed accommodation rather than reached restrictive territory, and a meeting gap before December gives the committee a reason to frontload restriction.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: A cheap asymmetric trade is paying up for October hike optionality in SOFR/fed funds futures while the market still prices a coin flip.
insights.quote: it feels a bit funny that we're only priced at 50% for October you know why would why would you know war talk about okay we've removed a bit of restrict or we've moved a bit of accommodation which means that they don't even think they're restrictive yet

insights.claim: The rates market is pricing roughly four hikes by the middle of next year against a Fed dot plot implying two, so the market is running a more aggressive tightening path than the Fed's own Summary of Economic Projections.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: The gap means hawkish Fed surprises are largely pre-paid; the pain trade in rates is a dovish repricing, not a hawkish one.
insights.quote: The market's currently at roughly four by mid mid next year

insights.claim: The core bearish argument of the episode is that the Fed is turning maximally hawkish and unconcerned about unemployment at what is likely peak growth, with a slowdown behind it.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Classic late-cycle setup: fade cyclical equities and steepeners priced for perpetual nominal growth, and watch for the Fed's forecast error to show up in Q1 data.
insights.quote: they're they're turning most hawkish into peak growth and what what could be a slowdown behind this

insights.claim: Deluard frames his own bearish turn as a contrarian signal precisely because the 'recessions are cancelled, permanent stimulus' view he once held alone has now become consensus across the entire Fed board, which historically marks regime change.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Use the unanimity of the high-nominal-growth narrative as a sentiment extreme; regime-change trades are cheapest when no one is hedging them.
insights.quote: it seems that the stuff that sounded crazy when we talked about it about two years ago, this idea that recessions are cancelled and this is kind of permanent stimulus

insights.claim: Warsh's inconsistent approach to forward guidance is itself a structural source of higher rates volatility, independent of the policy path.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Favor long-volatility structures in rates; the Fed reaction function is now a less reliable anchor for carry trades.
insights.quote: Worsh kind of dances between not giving forward guidance and giving forward guidance. So, that right there is a a reason for the increased volatility

insights.claim: Tightening has already been delivered by the market through a 5% 10-year yield and elevated distillate prices, raising the question of whether an additional fed funds hike adds anything beyond reflex.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: If market-delivered tightening is doing the work, the Fed risks over-tightening the same way it did before the fall-2024 panic cuts.
insights.quote: here we are again, you know, 5% 10 year diesel where it's at, like this is going to start to hit demand

insights.claim: Deluard argues the hike should be judged a 'forced mistake' rather than a policy error, because the market gave Warsh no alternative and not hiking would have produced a worse outcome.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Implies no quick reversal: the Fed cannot cut until the market's inflation/currency constraint relaxes, which caps the dovish-pivot trade.
insights.quote: if it's a mistake it was a forced mistake like the market did not leave him a choice you know if he didn't do it it would have been way worse

insights.claim: Quinn argues a hike can only be called a policy mistake if the preceding interventions in FX, bond and commodity markets are also called mistakes, because without them equities would have deflated the AI bubble on their own and rates hikes would never have been on the table.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Frames policy risk as a chain: each liquidity intervention raises the eventual level of rates needed, so intervention headlines are bearish duration over a 6-12 month horizon.

insights.claim: Quinn's preferred rebalancing mechanism is a much steeper yield curve to discipline profligate fiscal spending, noting the curve remains historically inverted and the current Fed moves are flattening it further.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Argues against consensus steepeners in the near term while identifying a steepener as the necessary eventual resolution; sizing and timing matter more than direction.
insights.quote: you you would want an even steeper yield curve that would put the governor on the the proflegate spending

insights.claim: Deluard totals roughly $300-400bn of what he calls 'stealth midterm stimulus' across the SPR release, individual tax refunds, tariff refunds and accelerated capex deductions, and argues it is now waning with no replacement.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Quantifies the fiscal impulse cliff into 2027; model consumption and earnings off a lower run-rate rather than extrapolating 2026 nominal strength.
insights.quote: so you put it all in you have about three to 400 billion of let's call that the stealth midterm stimulus

insights.claim: The accelerated capex deduction tied to the buildout reduced corporate income tax collections by roughly $100bn, making part of the reported earnings surge a fiscal transfer rather than productivity.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Adjusting earnings for this transfer lowers the quality of the AI-productivity narrative supporting current equity multiples.

insights.claim: Deluard estimates roughly $200bn of the fiscal package flowed straight into corporate profits, close to a double-digit share of aggregate US profits, meaning a large chunk of earnings growth rests on stimulus that will not be renewed next year.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Directly attacks the 2027 EPS bridge; forward estimates that assume AI-driven margin expansion are double-counting a one-off fiscal windfall.
insights.quote: a good chunk of that of that earnings growth that's really supporting the market right now is on the back of fiscal stimulus that is waning and will probably not be renewed next year

insights.claim: A near-record draining of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve functioned as a large and under-appreciated consumer stimulus by suppressing oil and pump prices ahead of the midterms.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: When SPR releases stop, the same mechanism reverses into a consumer headwind and an inflation tailwind; watch weekly SPR levels as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: what's not appreciated that much but is very big stimulus is a near record draining of the SPR that has kept oil prices lower, helped the consumer at the pump

insights.claim: Fed liquidity support has already been withdrawn quietly, with the repo facility operations falling from $40bn a month to zero while real rates rose across the whole curve.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Liquidity conditions are tightening on two axes at once; funding-sensitive assets (crypto, small caps, credit) are the first to feel it.
insights.quote: you've had a gradual worsening of Fed support as the RMPs have come completely off gone from 40 billion a month to zero

insights.claim: Real-time Daily Treasury Statement tax data shows personal income growth decelerating from about 10% at the start of the year to a mid-single-digit pace, with withheld receipts (less sensitive to capital gains) falling from roughly 6-7% to 4-5%.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: A high-frequency, unrevised confirmation of slowing nominal income that leads the official data; track withheld receipts weekly instead of waiting on BLS.
insights.quote: it's not catastrophic but it's definitely slowing and it's slowing steadily

insights.claim: Rising real rates transmit to growth data with a three-to-six month lag, so a decision made on current growth prints is a backward-looking decision.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Sets a concrete window: the tightening delivered now should show in data around Q1-Q2 2027, which is when the Fed's hawkish framing becomes vulnerable.
insights.quote: Real rates rise and then you see three to six months after the data starts slowing and everyone's surprised

insights.claim: A post-midterm divided Congress is expected to be more oriented toward taxation and regulation, less AI-friendly, and to leave the administration with less political capital for coercing allies on strategic resources, compounding the fading growth impulse into 2027.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Policy risk premium on AI capex names and on deficit-funded growth should rise as midterm odds firm up, not after the result.

insights.claim: The US has now run roughly six consecutive months of negative real wage growth, with nominal wages falling while inflation reaccelerated after the Iran war, despite what looks like full employment.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Negative real wages with tight labor is an unstable equilibrium; either wages catch up (second-round inflation) or consumption cracks, and both are bad for multiples.
insights.quote: so now we're looking at six months I think of of negative real wage uh growth and um it's kind of odd right I mean because we have full employment

insights.claim: Deluard offers a benign explanation for wage restraint - AI-displacement fear producing a Greenspan-style Phillips curve shift, analogous to 1990s fear of the internet - but assigns it lower probability than the alternative.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: If the benign case holds, current inflation is genuinely transitory and long duration is cheap; investors should treat wage prints as the deciding variable between the two regimes.
insights.quote: People are afraid that you know they'll be u fired and replaced by an AI bot. Therefore they kind of lay low uh and we can have um you know basically a shift in the Philips curve if you will

insights.claim: Deluard's base case is that wage demands return with a lag once the May rally's wealth effect fades and households confront depleted savings and higher costs, feeding the commodity shock into wages and then into services inflation.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Second-round effects would make the Fed's path much harder; favors inflation-linked exposure and real assets over nominal duration.
insights.quote: you see the cost of everything's exploded, your savings are depleted. Um, yeah, you're you're going to ask for the pay raise. I don't think it's that different this time

insights.claim: Deluard argues that stripping out the AI investment boom, the current US policy mix - erratic tariffs raising input costs, expensive wars, restricted immigration and no deficit action - has stagflation as its default outcome at the end of a long expansion.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Makes the AI capex boom the single load-bearing variable in the bull case; any deceleration exposes the underlying stagflationary policy mix.
insights.quote: we had very stagflationary policy if it hadn't been for this AI boom

insights.claim: Reduced immigration has lowered potential growth, leaving the economy less able to absorb supply shocks without generating inflation.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: A lower speed limit means the Fed reaches its inflation constraint at weaker growth rates; expect hawkish reactions to prints that would previously have been benign.

insights.claim: Headline strength such as the week's retail sales beat should be discounted as nominal, since years of above-2% inflation make current data far less clear-cut than a comparable slowdown in 2018.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Deflate every activity print before acting on it; nominal beats are a poor guide to real demand in this regime.
insights.quote: we had the retail sales data this week and it like beep like crazy. But we also got to remember that's like nominal

insights.claim: The economy is described as a stagflationary malaise with a few investment booms layered on top, in which policy cannot support everything at once - fixing one variable necessarily worsens another.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Predicts policy whipsaw rather than a clean cycle; favors relative-value and pair trades over directional macro bets.
insights.quote: we're in this sort of stagflationary malaise with a few different like investment booms tacked on top to keep things afloat

insights.claim: Sticky inflation is expected to persist through year-end because of oil, and if oil keeps rising it will flip from being primarily an inflation problem to primarily a growth problem.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: A specific regime marker to watch: once oil starts hitting demand rather than prices, the trade rotates from inflation hedges to recession hedges.
insights.quote: inflation's still sticky. So, and it's going to be through year end because of oil, which by the way, at some point here is going to start causing more growth problems than inflation problems if it keeps rising

themes.theme: Dead Housing Market, No Rate Relief

insights.claim: The US housing market is described as effectively dead with mortgage rates back at highs near 7%, removing the traditional lifeblood leg of the economy just as the AI capex boom decelerates on a rate-of-change basis.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: With housing and capex both fading, there is no third leg to lean on; homebuilders and housing-linked credit have no cyclical bid coming.
insights.quote: the housing market's effectively dead like the the mortgage rates are back to highs which we know kind of leads starts and and activity

insights.claim: The usual escape valve - a slowdown that lowers long rates and triggers a refinancing boom - is unlikely this cycle because the inflation problem plus a Treasury supply problem should keep long rates from falling precipitously even in a slowdown.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: Breaks the standard 'bad news is good news for housing' reflex; a growth scare may not deliver the duration rally that housing longs are underwriting.
insights.quote: I don't see rates coming down that precipitously even if we do slow because of both the inflation problem plus the the supply problem

insights.claim: Felix is explicitly fading his own dip-buying instinct, arguing things have to get worse before they get better because policymakers have few levers left to unlock housing short of new programs or new stimulus.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: A named risk to the short thesis: any new housing-specific program (mortgage subsidies, GSE action) would be the catalyst that invalidates it.

insights.claim: Polymarket odds of a Democratic midterm sweep moved from about 50 to 60 in roughly a week and are now the base case, which the hosts attribute in part to the $5,000 check proposal backfiring.
insights.speaker: Felix (host) and Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Prediction-market odds are the cleanest real-time proxy for the 2027 policy regime; rising sweep odds should compress valuations on deregulation- and AI-policy-sensitive names.
insights.quote: it went from 50 to 60 in like a week

insights.claim: The hosts find the administration's calm in the face of collapsing midterm odds genuinely unsettling, noting that in normal political crises you would see blame-shifting and defections rather than quiet confidence.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Flags an unmodeled tail: if the administration is calm because it does not expect a normal electoral process, political risk premia are mispriced.
insights.quote: why are they so calm, right? I mean, what why do we not see uh you know, the rats leaving the boat, the the backstabbing?

insights.claim: Deluard cites data he attributes to Louis-Vincent Gave of Gavekal showing Trump has spent almost none of his large campaign war chest, and speculates it is being reserved for post-election litigation over redistricting and contested results rather than for helping candidates.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Unspent campaign funds are a cheap leading indicator of a contested-election scenario, which would extend political uncertainty rather than resolve it in November.
insights.quote: Trump has not spent any of his back money or almost you know almost nothing of of his big war chess that he has

insights.claim: The administration began the year with populist measures like credit card rate caps and mortgage programs, caused market wobbles, reversed course toward corporate-friendly policy, and the hosts see that reversal showing up directly in deteriorating approval ratings.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Establishes the political reaction function: weak polls push the administration back toward market-unfriendly populism, a live risk to financials and consumer credit.

insights.claim: Both hosts flag a pre-midterm geopolitical shock or 'October surprise' as an explicitly non-base-case tail, while noting all the conditions for a larger market problem are in place.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Argues for owning cheap convexity into October rather than sizing up a directional view.
insights.quote: there's tons of all the conditions are there I think for a bigger problem in markets

insights.claim: Deluard argues that ending the Iran war matters more for inflation, equities and rates than anything monetary policy does, because ending it would dramatically expand policy degrees of freedom.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Peace headlines, not Fed headlines, are the highest-beta event risk; size commodity and rates positions around war de-escalation news.
insights.quote: what what really matters is the stupid war. I mean at the end of the day uh you know you want to know what's going to happen to inflation the stock market rates whatever I mean you you know you have to you have to end this war

insights.claim: Physical diesel stress is showing up, with reports of gas stations running out of diesel and distillate prices moving sharply, arriving at a politically worst-possible moment before the midterms.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: Distillate shortages hit freight and food costs fastest; a direct channel from the war into both headline inflation and midterm politics.
insights.quote: I saw a photo the other day of like gas stations starting to run out of diesel and like diesel is just going crazy

insights.claim: The hosts flag that the three leading frontier AI lab CEOs, who despise each other, all converged on the same strategic and regulatory direction in the same weekend, and treat the motive as economic rather than moral.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Coordinated lab messaging is a leading indicator of regulatory capture attempts; incumbents win and the capex narrative that supports the market may be about to change shape.
insights.quote: what is your guys' best tinfoil hat theory on why the the three leading Frontier Lab CEOs all who despise each other all started to agree on on, you know, strategic and regulatory direction last weekend?

insights.claim: Deluard reads the frontier-lab convergence through Adam Smith: three captains of industry in a room will rapidly reach consensus to corner the market, with the economic driver being that staying on the frontier is ruinously expensive and hard to put in an S-1.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: If labs collude to slow the frontier, capex growth decelerates faster than consensus and the semiconductor/power supply chain is the first casualty.
insights.quote: if you put uh three three captains of industry in in the same room uh very rapidly a consensus will emerge uh to basically corner the market

insights.claim: Deluard cites an imminent Anthropic IPO with a roughly $3 trillion prize as a structural reason the AI boom gets kept alive, and uses it as a check on his own bearishness.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: A named catalyst with enormous incentive alignment behind keeping risk appetite intact into the listing window; fading the AI complex before that IPO fights a powerful sponsor.
insights.quote: anthropic IPO is just around the corner which by the way I think is an argument to keep this going right because there's a $3 trillion prize so close you can almost touch it

insights.claim: Felix attributes the lab convergence to coincidentally aligned incentives rather than one cause: Anthropic pursuing regulatory capture ahead of its IPO, OpenAI delaying its IPO while amplifying fear, and Musk benefiting from a frontier slowdown because Grok sits in third place.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: Reading each lab's IPO timing as the tell on its policy stance gives a framework for anticipating the next regulatory push.
insights.quote: Elon supporting slowing down at the Frontier. I mean, Grock and his model is in third place right now. I think it would be in his best interest if the Frontier slowed down a bit so he could catch up

insights.claim: The hosts note the central risk of the lab convergence is that everything in the economy currently rests on the frontier not slowing down, so labs saying the quiet part out loud is itself bearish.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: Watch lab public statements as a macro variable, not a tech story; a credible frontier-slowdown signal removes the one growth leg the bears concede.
insights.quote: if we're talking about slowing down um that's probably not good for what the entire economy is dependent on continuing

insights.claim: Deluard's central decade-long macro call is that Europe today sits roughly where Japan was in 2012, and will eventually be forced into the same resolution: debasing its currency until tax collections grow faster than social spending.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Frames a multi-year structural short euro position analogous to the post-2012 yen trade, which ran for 15 years.
insights.quote: Europe today is very much where Japan is was uh in 2012

insights.claim: Deluard argues terms of trade is the underappreciated organizing concept - dismissed because it came from 1970s Marxist economists and was displaced by productivity and TFP - and that China simultaneously deflating industrial export prices while bidding up raw materials degraded Japanese and now European living standards.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Provides a screen for which economies face forced devaluation: adverse terms-of-trade shocks plus rigid social commitments equal currency adjustment.
insights.quote: how much you sell your exports is how much you have to pay your imports is super super important

insights.claim: Deluard dismisses the European productivity route - the Draghi competitiveness report and the Lisbon strategy - as magical thinking given an aging population, rising social spending and a broken economic model, leaving devaluation as the only remaining option.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Treat each new EU competitiveness initiative as noise rather than a catalyst; the real trigger is currency policy.
insights.quote: Every every five years we have a bold and brave new report, you know, the draggy report of competitiveness, the Lisbon strategy to turn the Europe into a super. It's not going to happen on its own

insights.claim: The yen went from an 80 handle to roughly 165, a nominal devaluation of more than 50% and close to 65% including the inflation differential, which Deluard calls the biggest consistently applied economic policy of the last 15 years outside the AI story.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Sets the magnitude template for what a European adjustment could look like: a multi-decade, 50%+ currency move, not a cyclical swing.
insights.quote: we had an an 80 handle on the yen at one point you know this summer when I was there it was 165 so nominally it was more than 50%

insights.claim: Deluard argues yen bears miss that Japan fixed its balance sheet: the primary budget is balanced, tax collections are growing 6%, and net of Bank of Japan holdings debt-to-GDP fell from roughly 200% to 150%.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Supports being long yen rather than short it, and makes Japanese assets the funding-side winner in the Europe/Japan pair.
insights.quote: net of the central bank holdings the beautiful deleveraging has happened it's gone from 200% of GDP to 150

insights.claim: Deluard applies the R-minus-G framework to argue Japan has no debt crisis because G exceeds R, whereas France is the shakiest case with G near zero and R at 4% and rising, with the US somewhat exposed too.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: A concrete sovereign-risk screen that puts French OATs, not JGBs, at the center of the next debt scare.

insights.claim: Headline European debt-to-GDP understates the problem because unfunded pension obligations are not accounted for, with studies putting France or Italy near 500% on a net-present-value basis.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Removes the 'Europe has fiscal room relative to Japan' counterargument and strengthens the case for currency adjustment as the release valve.
insights.quote: if you I've seen studies that you you know, France or Italy at 500% if if you if you do the net present value of the pension obligation

insights.claim: Deluard argues Japan's devaluation succeeded because of favorable conditions Europe will not get: first-mover advantage, a deflationary global backdrop, US tolerance for geopolitical reasons against China, a tight aligned policy circle under Abe and Kuroda, and a large foreign asset position that generated offsetting capital gains.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Predicts Europe's version arrives clumsily through political crisis rather than smooth policy, meaning more volatility and worse risk-adjusted entry points.
insights.quote: What Japan achieved from you know with with smart policies and determination I think Europe will achieve clumsily uh with uh with a sequence of of nasty political crisis

insights.claim: Deluard names the sequence of European catalysts: the French presidential election in the spring, then the German election, then a deep existential EU crisis.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Gives a calendar for the euro-debasement thesis; the spring French election is the first tradeable event.

insights.claim: Deluard's preferred expression is short euro against the yen, supplemented with long US dollar and long Brazilian real versus euro to fix the carry, since the collapsed rate differential makes the long-yen leg cheap to hold for a long time.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: A concrete, carry-adjusted structure for a multi-year thesis; the point is that negative carry usually kills structural FX trades and here it does not.
insights.quote: the cost of having that that short yen short euro long yen is very short because the the race differential of collapse right so that the carry is very small

insights.claim: Deluard points to gold priced in yen since 2012 as the template for what gold priced in euros would do under a European debasement.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Gold in EUR, rather than gold in USD, is the cleaner way to express the debasement trade if the dollar is simultaneously strong.
insights.quote: look at gold priced in yen uh since 2012

insights.claim: Quinn argues the real debasement trade is hiding in Europe rather than in US Treasury policy, because the dollar looks coiled to move higher given US advantages in energy, AI and capital flows, yet he remains bullish gold because countries are hiking into an energy shock.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson
insights.so_what: Reconciles a strong-dollar and long-gold view: own gold against the debasing currency, not against the dollar.
insights.quote: the debasement trade that everybody's looking at Besson and the buybacks, but really the debasement trade's hiding in Europe

insights.claim: The hosts argue an ECB hike has considerably more economic impact than a Fed hike, and doubt the ECB can push through more than another one or two hikes without breaking something.
insights.speaker: Quinn Thompson and Felix (host)
insights.so_what: Positions European rates as the more fragile side of the transatlantic policy divergence trade.
insights.quote: the ECB hiking is a lot more impact than the US hiking

insights.claim: Deluard sees the ECB under Lagarde as an obstacle rather than an enabler of the needed adjustment, contrasting her with Draghi and with the tight Abe-Kuroda alignment that made Japan's policy work, though he expects the ECB to capitulate once bonds become unsellable.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Implies the euro-debasement trade is back-loaded: it only works after a bond-market crisis forces the ECB's hand, so timing risk is real.
insights.quote: Yeah, Churchill's lines. You can count on politicians to do the right thing only after they've tried everything else

insights.claim: The structural obstacle to a European version of BOJ-style yield curve control is the original sin of a common currency with fragmented national debt markets, since the ECB must weigh German-Italian spreads in a way the BOJ never had to.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: BTP-Bund spread is the key instrument to watch as the transmission mechanism and constraint on any European monetization.
insights.quote: the the original sin of a common currency and, you know, fragmented debt markets is that it's a lot easier for the BOJ to say, "Hey, we're going to go buy a bunch of uh a bunch of bonds."

insights.claim: Deluard suggests a US-Europe deal is plausible under a future administration, in which Europe drops contentious policies and the US tolerates a weaker euro because letting the second-largest economy and export market collapse would invite Russia, Iran, Turkey and China to carve up an already fragmented Europe.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Identifies US acquiescence as the gating condition for the euro-debasement thesis, and a change of US administration as its likely trigger.

themes.theme: Hated UK Equities And Carney's Canada

insights.claim: Deluard argues the Swiss franc has stopped being the clean hedge against European crisis, because an escalating France-Germany breakdown would push so much money into Swiss banks that the SNB intervenes, leaving buyers indirectly holding the very bonds they were avoiding.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Undermines the default European-crisis hedge and creates demand for an alternative correlated-but-better expression.
insights.quote: the the SNB won't be able to won't tolerate u all the all the money being pushed in in the Swiss banking sector. They will intervene. So, you'll just be buying the bonds you don't want to touch uh via the SNB

insights.claim: Deluard's contrarian trade is long UK equities as a correlated-but-better pair against European crisis, citing that UK private-sector defined benefit pension funds have cut domestic equity allocations from 50% to 5%, meaning the selling is effectively done.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: A flow-exhaustion argument with a specific measurable trigger: any reversal in UK pension domestic allocation is the catalyst.
insights.quote: they used to own 50% in in UK equities. Uh now it's down to 5%. I mean this is insane

insights.claim: Deluard likes the UK index because it is concentrated in his three preferred sectors - energy, healthcare and financials - and is cheap and unloved, with universal derision of the idea treated as a positive signal.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Sector composition means the UK trade is also implicitly a long-energy, long-value expression rather than a pure country bet.
insights.quote: they are massively on their own they are cheap uh you look at the index it's exactly the three sectors that I like, energy, healthcare, and and then financials

insights.claim: Deluard argues the UK is roughly a decade ahead of the continent in this political crisis (Brexit preceded Trump) and, critically, has a single central bank giving it far more policy flexibility than the EU's 27-member decision process.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Institutional decision speed is the differentiating variable in the UK-versus-Europe pair, not valuation alone.
insights.quote: they have an they have a one central bank so they have a lot more policy flexibility than than Europe

insights.claim: Deluard advises watching for small, quiet European policy reversals rather than headlines - Norway resuming North Sea drilling and telling the European Commission no, an unfrozen exploration block, a lithium mine in Alsace - as the real early signals of change.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete watchlist of micro-signals to time entry into European resource and industrial exposure ahead of official policy shifts.
insights.quote: I would want like small Oh huh they unfroze a block for exploration in North Sea that's interesting they open a lithium mine in in Alzas

insights.claim: Felix argues Carney is being misread as the 2020 Davos 'Values' author and is in practice pragmatic, combining fiscal conservatism with social liberalism, with rising approval ratings and weekly consultation with former Conservative PM Stephen Harper, who appointed him to the Bank of Canada.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: Supports a constructive view on Canadian assets on the grounds that policy execution is more market-friendly than the label suggests.

insights.claim: Canada is shifting from a decade in which the economy was, as Felix describes it, essentially a real estate Ponzi scheme plus an education scam, toward attracting foreign capital investment, with the ESG mandate era for pensions described as over and Harper now heading the Alberta pension fund.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: A large domestic pension pool redirecting from ESG mandates toward natural resources is a durable bid for Canadian energy and materials.
insights.quote: our our economy for the last decade was just a real estate Ponzi scheme basically

insights.claim: Felix argues Canada has real fiscal capacity with a deficit lower than many peers, enabling a large investment and capex stimulus push, and retains retaliatory leverage over the US through exports such as potash even though Trump could still force a significant recession.
insights.speaker: Felix (host)
insights.so_what: Fiscal room plus resource leverage plus a strongly performing TSX makes Canada the developed-market equity story the hosts are most constructive on.

insights.claim: Deluard says he should add long Canadian dollar to his short euro position, citing Canada's natural resource position as making the pair interesting.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Extends the short-euro basket into a commodity-currency leg, adding resource beta to the structural European debasement trade.
insights.quote: I should add a long CAD to my short EUR trade

insights.claim: Deluard views Canada's policy response to US pressure as globally important because Europeans do not take initiative on their own and will copy Carney's approach if it visibly works.
insights.speaker: Vincent Deluard, StoneX
insights.so_what: Makes Canadian policy outcomes a leading indicator for the timing of European reform, and therefore for the euro thesis.
insights.quote: I think the can to some extent the fate of the world rest upon can Canada
